summary: From the highest peaks of the Southern Alps/Kā Tiritiri o te Moana to the wild beaches of the West Coast, Westland Tai Poutini packs glaciers, rainforest, lakes and wetlands into a short drive on State Highway 6. Franz Josef Glacier/Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere and Fox Glacier/Te Moeka o Tuawe end in rainforest less than 300 metres above the sea, and Lake Matheson mirrors Aoraki/Mount Cook on still mornings.
story: The Alpine Fault splits the park. East of it the mountains rise suddenly, their steep forested slopes cut by impassable gorges, and high above them permanent snowfields feed a mass of glaciers. Two of them, Franz Josef and Fox, descend right down to the lowlands; their terminal faces lie less than 300 metres above sea level. In the last ice age they joined a great ice sheet that reached beyond the present coastline. Fox Glacier/Te Moeka o Tuawe, 13 kilometres long, is one of the longest in the park.

West of the fault, dense rainforest covers the lowlands, and nearer the coast lie lakes, wetlands and wide river mouths. The threatened kāmana/crested grebe lives on Lake Māpōurika, and Ōkārito Lagoon is famous for the kōtuku/white heron. In the heart of the lowland forest lives the only population of rowi, New Zealand's rarest kiwi. Kea are common throughout the park. Where retreating ice has left rubble behind, rātā and kāmahi forest takes hold within a century; on bare rock, lichens and mosses take far longer.

Early Māori settlements clung to the shores of Westland's lakes and lagoons, where food was plentiful, and Ngāi Tahu travelling the coast in search of pounamu came to know the glaciers, peaks and forests well. Gold changed the coast quickly. In 1864–65 at least 16,000 miners arrived; in the spring of 1865 gold was found in the black beach sands, and towns sprang up at Ōkārito, Five Mile and Gillespies, only to empty within eighteen months. Julius von Haast reached the Franz Josef valley in 1865, when Sentinel Rock had just emerged from the ice.

Visitors followed the surveyors. By the early 1900s so many tourists came that the Government paid hoteliers to build tracks and huts, and guides such as Peter and Alec Graham led parties onto the ice. The Copland Track was built across the Alps between about 1901 and 1913. Westland National Park was proclaimed on 29 March 1960, and the park grew in 1982, 1983, 2002 and 2010 as lowland forests and whole valleys were added. It is part of Te Wāhipounamu – South West New Zealand World Heritage Area.
howItWorks: Westland Tai Poutini is public conservation land run by the Department of Conservation (DOC), and there is no entry fee: under the National Parks Act 1980 the public has freedom of entry and access, within the rules that protect the park. The townships of Franz Josef/Waiau and Fox Glacier/Weheka sit on the park boundary and provide the accommodation, fuel and shops; DOC's visitor centre is in Franz Josef. DOC has begun charging for parking at the Franz Josef Glacier car park, the one fee most day visitors will meet.

The glaciers are retreating and the valleys below them change every day. Glacial rivers can be dammed by ice falls and burst, flooding the valley floor; rock falls from the valley walls after rain; ice can collapse at the terminal face. The walks end at viewpoints hundreds of metres from the ice, with barriers and signs that mark the limit of safe access, and people have died or been badly hurt after crossing them. Getting closer to or onto the glaciers means going with one of the guiding companies in Franz Josef and Fox Glacier; helicopters are now the only safe way onto the ice. Check the daily glacier access update on the Glacier Country website before you go.

Overnight trips use DOC huts. Welcome Flat Hut on the Copland Track is a serviced hut that must be booked, with fees that rise in summer and at weekends; most other backcountry huts are first come, first served, paid with hut tickets or a Backcountry Hut Pass. The park's high alpine huts are serviced alpine huts with their own fees, for mountaineers. Dogs are not allowed in the park, and flying a drone needs a DOC permit.

sights.name: Franz Josef Glacier/Kā Roimata o Hine Hukatere
sights.note: A 30-minute return walk through rainforest to a view up the glacier valley. The Waiho River has cut off access further up; never go past the barriers.

sights.name: Sentinel Rock
sights.note: A glacier-smoothed schist knoll in the Franz Josef valley, with views of the glacier, the valley and the Waiho River. Ice pressed against nearby Harper Rock until 1909.

sights.name: Roberts Point
sights.note: A challenging 12.3-kilometre return hike past historic Hende's Gallery to a lookout high above the Franz Josef ice. Unbridged creeks and slippery slabs; choose a dry day.

sights.name: Alex Knob
sights.note: An eight-hour return climb from rainforest to alpine meadows, with what DOC calls the best views of Franz Josef Glacier without a helicopter. Start early to beat the afternoon cloud.

sights.name: Fox Glacier/Te Moeka o Tuawe
sights.note: The South Side Walkway follows the Fox River through podocarp forest to a glacier viewpoint, 6.4 km return. The glacier is the moeka, final resting place, of Tuawe.

sights.name: Lake Matheson/Te Ara Kairaumati
sights.note: A glacier-formed lake whose dark water mirrors Aoraki/Mount Cook and Mount Tasman/Te Horokōau on calm days. A 4.4-km loop; the first section to Jetty Lookout suits wheelchairs.

sights.name: Ōkārito Lagoon
sights.note: A wide coastal lagoon on the park's northern edge, famous for the kōtuku/white heron; the old gold-rush settlement of Ōkārito stands beside it.

sights.name: Lake Māpōurika
sights.note: A lake north of Franz Josef/Waiau, home to the threatened kāmana/crested grebe.

sights.name: Welcome Flat hot pools
sights.note: Natural hot pools by Welcome Flat Hut, seven hours up the Copland Track, facing the Sierra Range. No soap, no digging; keep your head above water.

sights.name: Westland Tai Poutini National Park Visitor Centre
sights.note: DOC's visitor centre at 69 Cron Street, Franz Josef/Waiau, for weather, track conditions and the region's history; the historic Cape Defiance Hut is on display here.

entrances: Franz Josef/Waiau on SH6 — the visitor centre, and the 4 km Glacier Access Road or Te Ara a Waiau Walkway/Cycleway to the glacier car park
Fox Glacier/Weheka on SH6 — the South Side Walkway, 2 km south of the township, and Lake Matheson, about 6 km towards the coast
The Copland Track car park beside the Karangarua River bridge on SH6, 26 km south of Fox Glacier
Ōkārito, on the coast at the northern edge of the park
planYourVisit.reservations: No booking is needed to enter the park. Welcome Flat Hut and its campsite on the Copland Track must be booked and paid for in advance; the Copland Track can close at short notice in heavy rain, and DOC emails people with bookings. Check glacier access and track conditions at the visitor centre or on the daily glacier access update before you go.
permits: Flying a drone needs a DOC permit
Recreational gold fossicking on the Waiho riverbed between the Callery Gorge suspension bridge and the Waiho road bridge needs no permit; hand tools only
Hunting on conservation land needs a DOC hunting permit
camping: A booked campsite outside Welcome Flat Hut on the Copland Track
No camping at the Copland Track road end
lodging: Hotels, motels and campgrounds in Franz Josef/Waiau and Fox Glacier/Weheka, and accommodation at Ōkārito
Welcome Flat Hut, a 31-bunk serviced hut, and the Sierra Room inside it for groups of up to four
Serviced alpine huts such as Almer, Centennial, Chancellor and Pioneer for mountaineers
seasonalClosures: Glacier walks, the Glacier Access Road and the Copland Track close at short notice for flooding, rockfall or landslides — check before you go
In winter, snow is likely above Christmas Lookout on the Alex Knob Track

weather: The park lies in the path of the prevailing westerly winds, which can bring heavy rain in any month — up to five metres falls in a year — and conditions change dramatically in a short time. Downpours can flood the glacier valleys within minutes, and a cold down-draught off the ice is normal even on fine days. In summer, afternoon cloud often hides the high country, so climb early; Lake Matheson's reflections are best at dawn and dusk on still, sunny days. In winter snow is likely on high tracks such as Alex Knob. Carry warm, waterproof clothing at all times, and insect repellent, because sandflies are everywhere.
directions: The only road access is State Highway 6, from Hokitika in the north, about an hour and a half's drive, or from Haast in the south, about two hours; Fox Glacier township is 171 km south of Hokitika. The closest commercial airport is Hokitika, with daily flights from Christchurch, and regular buses run along the coast. The glacier car parks are a short drive from the two townships; the Franz Josef access road is unsealed but suitable for cars, campervans and buses.

fees.title: Franz Josef Glacier car park
fees.detail: NZ$20 a day; free if you leave within 10 minutes. Card only at the machines; locals can buy an annual permit online. As listed by DOC in November 2026; check before you go.

fees.title: Welcome Flat Hut, 1 October – 30 April
fees.detail: NZ$36 at weekends; from 1 December to 29 February NZ$38 on weekdays and NZ$40 at weekends; NZ$30 from 1 May to 30 September. Booked and paid in advance; hut tickets are not accepted, and a Backcountry Hut Pass only from May to September. As listed by DOC in November 2026.

fees.title: Standard and serviced backcountry huts
fees.cost: NZ$15 / NZ$25 per adult per night
fees.detail: The standard and serviced hut rates DOC listed in November 2026; individual huts can differ, so check each hut's page. A 12-month Backcountry Hut Pass is NZ$140 for an adult.

chronology.text: At least 16,000 miners arrive on the coast in the West Coast gold rush.
Gold is found in the black beach sands; Julius von Haast visits the Franz Josef valley.
New Zealand forms the world's first government tourism department, which goes on to build the Copland Track (completed about 1913).
Peter Hende builds Hende's Gallery, a walkway hung from iron bars on the cliffs on the way to Roberts Point.
Westland National Park is proclaimed by Order in Council at Greymouth on 29 March.
The southern part of Ōkārito State Forest and Waikukupa State Forest are added to the park.
The whole catchment of the upper Karangarua Valley is added.
With Aoraki/Mount Cook and Fiordland, the park forms New Zealand's first World Heritage Area.
Te Wāhipounamu – South West New Zealand World Heritage Area is established in December, taking in the park.
North Ōkārito and Saltwater state forests join the park; further additions follow in 2010.

safety: Never cross the barriers in the glacier valleys. River surges, flash floods, rock fall and ice collapse can come without warning, and people have died beyond the ropes.
Do not cross the Waiho or Callery rivers on foot — use the road bridge. On the Copland Track, turn back if Rough Creek is rising, and use the flood bridge upstream to get out.
Rock slabs on Roberts Point and Alex Knob are treacherous when wet or icy; choose a dry day and wear boots with good grip.
At Welcome Flat hot pools, keep your head above the water to avoid the risk of amoebic meningitis.
regulations: No dogs or other pets in the national park.
Flying a drone without a DOC permit is prohibited.
Gold fossicking only in the designated Waiho riverbed area, and only with hand-held tools.
Do not feed kea or other wildlife.
Check, clean and dry all gear when moving between waterways, to stop the spread of didymo and other freshwater pests.
